data.title: Dollar edges off 19-month high after market rout; yen softens
data.description:
By Gregor Stuart Hunter

The dollar eased off its highest level in more than a year and a half at the start of Asian trade on Monday, as investor confidence recovered after a selloff last week and traders pared bets that the Federal Reserve could hike interest rates aggressively at its meeting next month.

The euro was up 0.1% at $1.0974, while the Australian dollar was 0.2% stronger at $0.6629. The British pound was flat at $1.3091, while the New Zealand dollar was steady at $0.5474. The US dollar was up 0.2% against the yen at 158.63 yen as a safe-haven bid for the Japanese currency eased.

The US dollar index , which measures the greenback's strength against a basket of six currencies, was flat at 103.80, retreating from its highest levels since April 2025.

"We expect the USD to continue to outperform," said Eric Robertsen, global head of foreign exchange, rates and credit research at Standard Chartered in Dubai, citing interest rate differentials, signs of strong productivity gains in the US economy and a relative decline in political risk compared to other countries such as France. "If global risk aversion were to pick up, the USD should benefit as well."

After last week's market rout, aggressive action from the Fed to fight inflation now looks to be off the table.

Fed funds futures are pricing an implied 88.6% probability of a 25-basis-point hike at the US central bank's December 8-9 policy meeting, compared with an 11.4% chance of a hold, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. A larger 50-basis-point increase, seen as carrying an 11.5% likelihood a week ago, is now completely priced out.

Cryptocurrencies pared a rebound from a sharp drop on Friday, with bitcoin down 0.1% at $60,795.03 and ether 0.2% lower at $1,714.96.

data.title: US futures bounce while Asia markets brace for AI wipeout
data.description:
US stock futures bounced at the open on Monday, while Asian markets braced for more selling as authorities around the region readied support measures after a withering wipeout last week for tech and chip stocks at the centre of the AI boom.

Investors are questioning whether the vast sums of mostly borrowed money spent building data centres to power AI models will generate returns fast enough to repay lenders and big enough to justify some of the high stock prices.

Last week's 10% drop in the Nasdaq was its largest weekly drop since pandemic panic gripped markets in March 2020.

Nasdaq 100 futures bounced about 2% in early trade on Monday, and S&P 500 futures rose around 1%.

Japan markets are closed for a holiday on Monday but futures indicate selling pressure, while Hang Seng futures (HSIc1) also point to a fall. Australian stocks were 0.5% lower.

The "AI trade" has for several years lifted a wide range of stocks, from switch and cable makers to electricity generators and the manufacturers of anything in the computing supply chain, but they have been under pressure in recent months from rising interest rates.

AI-related shares took a particularly sharp downturn last week as the exit of Jensen Huang, the Nvidia CEO nicknamed the "godfather of AI", and the faltering debut of AI company Anthropic , which closed 8.5% lower on its first full day of trading, pointed to a souring mood.

Taiwanese shares TWSE:TAIEX were down 17% for the week, their biggest weekly fall since 1990, and Friday's 10% drop for the Philadelphia semiconductor index points to more pain for Asia's chip-heavy markets, especially in Taiwan and South Korea.

Taiwan's financial regulator on Saturday ordered a further tightening of short-selling rules for stocks, while in China stock exchanges announced a batch of support measures such as easing requirements for margin financing.

South Korea will be ready to deploy market stabilisation funds immediately should the market continue to fall, the finance ministry said on Sunday, after the benchmark index last week slumped to 10-month lows.

data.title: A $2 million exploit leads to a $3.7 million free-for-all as traders empty Fusionist’s ACE bridge
data.description:
An attacker made off with about $2 million on Sunday by minting a massive quantity of unbacked ACE (ACE) tokens, a creation of blockchain game project Fusionist, on BNB Chain and selling them for USDT while crashing ACE's price on the network, according to The Block's analysis of onchain data.

Traders then took the same cheap tokens, which by then numbered in the billions, and sent them through Fusionist's bridge, emptying it of its 53.7 million real ACE, worth about $3.7 million at current prices, onchain data shows. ACE's circulating supply before the exploit was only around 116 million tokens.

Fusionist is a blockchain gaming studio backed by Binance Labs (now YZi Labs) that makes sci-fi strategy games and runs its own blockchain, Endurance. ACE is the project's native token, which is used to pay transaction fees on Endurance. It trades on exchanges including Binance and OKX. A copy of the ACE token also exists as a separate token on BNB Chain. Fusionist runs a bridge that converts ACE between the two blockchains.

The exploit

Onchain analytics account Onchain Lens said on X that the attacker "exploited Fusionist's privileged bridge-minter access" to mint unbacked ACE and swap it for USDT, then routed $1.87 million through crypto mixer Tornado Cash. The Block traced about 1,150 ETH, worth roughly $2 million, into Tornado Cash from wallets that either received the minted ACE directly from the bridge or collected proceeds from its sale. The attacker moved the funds from BNB Chain to Ethereum through cross-chain swap services including SwftSwap and Relay.

The first mint, of 3.5 million ACE, came at 12:55 p.m. ET, according to BscScan data. ACE has a maximum supply of 147 million tokens. The mints grew to billions, then trillions, then quadrillions of ACE over the next two and a half hours, ending with a 10 quintillion ACE mint at 3:28 p.m.

The mints were sent from a wallet that Fusionist's deployer funded nearly three years ago, BscScan data shows. Blockchain security firm Blockaid, which first flagged the exploit, listed that wallet among the exploiter addresses.

The attacker sold each batch into decentralized exchange pools on BNB Chain as soon as it was minted. By 1:41 p.m. ET, one trader was able to buy ACE there for about $0.0001, compared with the roughly $0.04 price of ACE on exchanges at the time.

The free-for-all

Fusionist's bridge holds ACE tokens on its Endurance network to back the tokens on BNB Chain. When a user sends BNB Chain ACE back to the bridge, it burns those tokens and releases the same amount of ACE on Endurance. The bridge kept working after the attack, so any trader could buy the crashed tokens on BNB Chain and swap them for real ACE tokens, then sell them on exchanges.

From 1:13 p.m. to 3:05 p.m. ET, the Endurance contract paid out about 53.7 million ACE to 24 addresses, according to Endurance block explorer data. One address alone received 26.1 million, nearly a quarter of ACE's former circulating supply.

The bridge held about 53.7 million ACE before the hack; by Sunday afternoon it held only 0.08 ACE. Another 27 attempted transfers, totaling roughly 1.36 billion ACE, failed because the bridge was already nearly empty by that point.

Pseudonymous X user ZAMA_APPLE was the first to post about a user exploiting the arbitrage, sharing a screenshot that showed a trader turning $60 into $17,000 by buying ACE on BNB Chain and selling it on OKX. The Block traced the trade to a single wallet.

The wallet started with about $50 in USDT, withdrawn from Binance around 1:34 p.m. ET. It spent $10 testing the bridge, then used its remaining $40 to buy about 404,000 ACE at 1:41 p.m. Four minutes later, the bridge paid out the same amount of real ACE on Endurance, and the trader sent it straight to the exchange. By 1:53 p.m., it had sold the tokens for about $17,670, a 350x return.

Fusionist told its followers at 2:30 p.m. ET to pause ACE transfers, trades and bridging on BSC while it investigates "an apparent ongoing exploit." Fusionist has not posted an update since, as of publication time.

Crypto exchange Gate said its security team confirmed the bridge was exploited and that it would roll back all ACE/USDT trades executed between 12:55 p.m. and 2:15 p.m. ET. Gate also switched its ACE perpetual futures market to reduce-only and said it would settle and delist the market late Monday.

Some Gate users who sold ACE during that window were left with negative balances after Gate rolled back their trades, returning their ACE and reclaiming the USDT from the sales, Gate's support account said on X.

ACE is down about 20% over the past 24 hours, trading at roughly $0.069, according to The Block's price page. The Block has reached out to Fusionist and OKX for comment.

data.title: Beijing to bar young 'red-chip' firms from listing outside mainland China, sources say
data.description:
Key points:
  • Red-chip firms must redomicile in China before they can list offshore, sources say
  • Red-chip firms are registered abroad but control assets and businesses in China
  • Beijing has been gradually tightening oversight of capital raising by red-chip firms

China's securities watchdog has told some law firms it will not approve plans by red-chip firms to list outside mainland China, people familiar with the matter said, a move that tightens its control of capital raised offshore and could dent Hong Kong's IPO market.

Red-chip companies are registered abroad, mainly in tax havens, but control assets and businesses in China via equity ownership or contractual agreements.

The structure is favoured by Chinese startups, particularly tech firms, keen to raise capital in places like Hong Kong or New York to take advantage of more relaxed rules and deeper pools of funds available from foreign investors.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) has told law firm representatives in recent days that red-chip companies established after the introduction of new offshore listing rules in 2023 must be re-domiciled in China before they can list offshore, said the people.

The people declined to be identified as the regulatory guidance was confidential. The move is being reported for the first time by Reuters.

China and the US are competing fiercely to gain the upper hand in tech, particularly in AI and semiconductors, which has led to efforts by Chinese authorities to sharpen their scrutiny of technology, data and capital going outside its borders.

The CSRC did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Oversight of red-chip firms has gradually become stricter.

Prior to March 2023, Chinese companies employing overseas holding structures to raise capital abroad did not need regulatory approval. That changed with the advent of the new rules.

Then this year, the CSRC told Reuters in March that it was examining the "necessity and compliance" of red-chip structures, particularly those formed after March 2023.

Despite that warning, some red-chip IPO hopefuls and their advisors have been seeking approval to list outside the mainland without dismantling their existing structure and shifting their domicile back to China, one of the people said.

Most of those applicants failed to convince the regulator that a red-chip structure was necessary, prompting the tougher stance, the person added.

HONG KONG IPO MARKET COULD BE HURT

A drop-off in listings from red-chip firms is likely to hurt but not hobble Hong Kong, the top IPO destination for Chinese firms, which has seen business boom for the past 18 months.

Funds raised via IPOs in Hong Kong during the first 10 months of this year surged 84% from the same period last year to hit HK$404 billion ($52 billion), though the CSRC has slowed approvals of IPOs since September.

In addition to going slow on approvals for listings by AI, chip and humanoid robot firms after a market frenzy in those sectors, it has more broadly increased its scrutiny as markets have weakened.

Last year, one-fifth of 131 Hong Kong listings approved by the CSRC involved offshore holdings, the majority of which used a red-chip structure, according to Chinese law firm Han Kun.

So far this year, the CSRC has approved Hong Kong listings for just 6 red-chip companies, a sharp decline from 50 approved last year, according to data compiled by law firms and Reuters.

There were nearly 600 listing applications pending in Hong Kong at the end of October, official data showed.

Most of them are mainland Chinese firms though it was not clear how many are red chips given that the number includes applications that were filed confidentially.

There are, however, at least four active Hong Kong IPO applicants which have an offshore holding company structure for their mainland China businesses, according to a Reuters review of filings with the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Any red-chip firms seeking to list in Hong Kong or New York could now face a long wait before coming to market due to the time and costs involved in becoming incorporated in China.

But some, like Chinese AI firm StepFun, have been working on shifting their domicile back to China to pave the way for a planned overseas listing, sources have said. StepFun did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Asked about news of the ban on red-chip firms listing outside mainland China, the Hong Kong bourse said it "welcomes issuers with a range of ownership structures, provided they meet all applicable regulatory requirements in Hong Kong and other relevant jurisdictions."

($1 = 7.8410 Hong Kong dollars)
